tldr: This paper presents "Instruct-to-Act," an embodied agent framework that loosely couples the reasoning and planning capabilities of pretrained VLMs (Vision-Language Models) with the fast low-level control of world-model RL via natural language, achieving high accuracy and real-time execution without expert demonstrations.
hero_caption: Inference flow of Instruct-to-Act: The low-latency world-model controller continuously executes environment actions at high frequency, while the VLM planner reasons asynchronously in the background and intermittently emits high-level text instructions ($x_0, x_1$).
overview:
When operating robots or gaming agents, balancing high-level situational judgment and long-horizon planning with high-frequency, unbroken continuous control has been a long-standing challenge. State-of-the-art VLMs excel at commonsense understanding and plan decomposition, but their inference is heavy, making it impossible to continuously generate millisecond-level action sequences in unfamiliar environments. On the other hand, world-model RL controllers like Dreamer run extremely fast and smoothly, but steering them with open-ended natural language instructions has remained difficult.

To bridge this gap, the authors developed "Instruct-to-Act," a framework that cleanly decouples planning and control via a natural language instruction interface. The key idea is to take action trajectories collected by the controller itself, have a VLM summarize "what was done" in hindsight to automatically relabel them with synthetic text instructions, and jointly train the controller using behavior cloning (BC) alongside reinforcement learning objectives. This produces a language-instructable controller without requiring any human expert demonstrations. Furthermore, during inference, the planner's language reasoning and the controller's low-level execution run asynchronously in parallel.

Evaluated across seven diverse environments—including Minecraft, Atari, and cooperative multi-agent games—Instruct-to-Act significantly outperforms direct VLM action generation and non-instructed controller baselines. It remains competitive with strong vision-language-action (VLA) models and multi-agent RL methods on six of the seven tasks. The authors also demonstrate the plug-and-play flexibility of swapping in different pretrained VLM planners without any fine-tuning and without sacrificing inference throughput.
contributions: Decoupled the VLM planner (long-horizon planning) from the world-model controller (high-frequency control) via natural language, enabling plug-and-play operation without fine-tuning the VLM.

Established a training pipeline for language-instructable controllers without expert demonstrations by relabeling the controller's own rollout trajectories in hindsight using a VLM and combining it with behavior cloning (BC).
Designed an asynchronous inference pipeline that keeps the controller running without waiting for the VLM's reasoning to finish, eliminating the bottleneck caused by VLM inference latency.
Evaluated across seven diverse environments spanning single-agent to cooperative multi-agent setups, demonstrating both high task success rates and outstanding throughput.

sections.heading: Connecting a Thinking Mind and Fast Limbs with Natural Language
sections.summary: The authors propose "Instruct-to-Act," a novel approach that combines the strong planning abilities of VLMs with the fast, accurate low-level control of world-model RL. By decoupling planning and control through language, pretrained VLMs can be used directly as embodied agents without per-environment fine-tuning.
sections.details:
In environments like Minecraft that require long-term exploration, real-time control, and interaction with other players, two capabilities are essential: high-frequency, low-latency continuous control, and high-level reasoning and planning tailored to the situation.

Existing approaches remain divided. World-model RL algorithms like Dreamer acquire smooth low-level control with high sample efficiency directly from pixel inputs, but struggle to accept abstract, open-ended task guidance. Conversely, pretrained VLM and VLA models excel at decomposing tasks and setting subgoals from visual contexts, but their inference is too heavy to reliably produce continuous action sequences under strict control cycles.

Instruct-to-Act decouples decision-making into a "planner" and a "controller." A pretrained VLM planner intermittently issues text instructions from images, while a lightweight, environment-specific controller receives those instructions and generates actions at high frequency. The controller is built as a world model conditioned on language embeddings. By summarizing and relabeling its own rollout trajectories with a VLM in hindsight, it gains the ability to follow natural language instructions without extra expert data. Moreover, running planner reasoning and controller execution asynchronously eliminates the waiting time inherent to VLM inference.

captions.F1: Overview of the proposed inference architecture. The VLM planner reasons in the background to generate draft plans ($Pn$) and instructions ($x$), while the controller (Ctrl.) follows the latest instruction to output actions ($a_t$) and stop signals ($p_t^{\text{stop}}$) at each step.

sections.heading: Basic Setup: No VLM Fine-Tuning Required for the Environment
sections.summary: Instead of fine-tuning the VLM directly into the environment's action space, the authors formulate a hierarchical RL-style framework where sparse natural language instructions drive a lightweight controller. The method is evaluated across seven single-agent and multi-agent environments.
sections.details:
The goal of this work is to deploy existing instruction-tuned VLMs out-of-the-box as embodied agents without fine-tuning them to environment-specific action spaces.

In a Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (POMDP), the policy $\pi$ is modeled as a composition of a planner $\pi_p: \Omega \rightarrow \Delta^{\mathcal{X}}$ and a controller $\pi_c: \Omega \times \mathcal{X} \rightarrow \Delta^{\mathcal{A}}$, where $\Omega$ is the observation space, $\mathcal{A}$ is the low-level action space, and $\mathcal{X}$ is the set of natural language strings. While this resembles hierarchical reinforcement learning (HRL) or the options framework, high-level guidance here is expressed as free-form natural language.

The controller $\pi_c$ consists of an instruction-conditioned Recurrent State Space Model (RSSM) equipped with a dedicated output head to detect task completion. It can also act autonomously when no instruction is provided, and it is trained entirely via hindsight relabeling of self-generated rollouts without human demonstrations. The evaluation benchmark spans seven environments: classic single-agent RL domains including Atari, Crafter, DeepMind Lab, and MineRL, along with cooperative multi-agent environments including Overcooked, Pico Park, and MindCraft.

sections.heading: Asynchronous Inference and Hindsight Relabeling on Self-Generated Data
sections.summary: By pairing asynchronous inference—where VLM planning and controller execution run completely in parallel—with hindsight supervised instruction learning using VLM summaries, the framework achieves both high throughput and strong instruction-following capabilities.
sections.details:
The core technical innovations of this method lie in its asynchronous inference runtime and self-supervised hindsight relabeling during training.

### 3.1 & 3.3 Asynchronous Online Inference and Multi-Agent Coordination
If the planner only begins thinking after the controller finishes, VLM generation latency causes the agent to freeze at every transition. Instruct-to-Act resolves this by running the planner continuously in the background, updating draft plans ($Pn$) and reasoning memory ($Mr$) ahead of time based on a real-time observation stream. The moment the controller emits a task completion signal ($p_t^{\text{stop}}$), the planner quickly issues the next instruction from the draft in just a few tokens.
In multi-agent environments, each agent runs an independent VLM planner and controller thread. Coordination is achieved without centralized value functions, relying purely on natural language communication (claiming subgoals or negotiating roles) in a shared chat room.

### 3.2 Controller Architecture
The controller employs a DreamerV3-style RSSM. Text instructions $x_t$ are converted into an embedding vector $e_t$ using a frozen compact language model (MiniLM) and concatenated with the RSSM's latent state before feeding into policy and value heads. When no instruction is present, a learnable null embedding ensures autonomous behavior. A small head is also added to output an instruction completion probability $p_t^{\text{stop}} = \sigma(g(s_t, e_t))$.

### 3.4 Training with Hindsight Instruction Relabeling
Instead of collecting expert demonstrations, trajectory segments $[u_k, v_k]$ are randomly sampled from the controller's own replay buffer. The surrounding visual frames and action sequence are fed into a VLM summarizer (GPT-4o) to generate a concise command $x$ that describes what the behavior accomplished. Using $x$ as ground truth, the controller optimizes a behavior cloning loss $\mathcal{L}_{\text{bc}}$ and a stop prediction loss $\mathcal{L}_{\text{stop}}$ jointly with Dreamer's standard world-model, value, and policy losses. Relabeling only 50% of the buffer and leaving the rest uninstructed enables both reward-maximizing autonomy and language compliance.

captions.F5: Action summarization prompt used for controller training. Given frame sequences and action histories from a sampled segment, it filters out redundant button spam and outputs concise imperative instructions (6–18 tokens) capturing intentional behavior in JSON format.

sections.heading: High Task Performance and Blazing Execution Speed Across Seven Environments
sections.summary: Experiments across seven environments including Minecraft and Atari show that Instruct-to-Act significantly outperforms direct action-generating VLMs and uninstructed RL. It also demonstrates zero-shot swappability of VLM planners, strong multi-agent coordination, and high inference speed.
sections.details:
### 4.1 & 4.2 Experimental Setup
The controller mainly uses an 800M-parameter RSSM, with CLIP and DINOv2 visual features and MiniLM as the text encoder. Training took an average of 23 hours (up to 36 hours) per environment on 4x RTX A6000 GPUs. Hindsight relabeling overhead was modest, adding only ~17% in GPU hours and reducing training speed by 12%.

### 4.3 VLM Planner Performance
In the main results (Table 1), Instruct-to-Act matched or outperformed strong domain-specific baselines (such as JARVIS-1 in MineRL and specialized MARL baselines) in six of the seven environments. Compared to an end-to-end baseline where GPT-4o directly outputs low-level actions, Instruct-to-Act achieved dramatic score improvements across all tasks. Adding language subgoals also produced substantial gains over the controller alone without instructions (equivalent to DreamerV3). Using GPT-4o or Qwen-VL-2.5-72B as the planner yielded the highest overall performance.

### 4.4 Scalability and Execution Efficiency
Comparing inference throughput in Minecraft Diamond, online asynchronous planning not only improved task performance over synchronous offline waiting, but also preserved orders-of-magnitude faster throughput (steps/s). In Pico Park multi-agent scaling (from 2 to 8 players), decentralized chat negotiation among planners maintained high throughput and achieved higher completion rates than a single centralized planner, demonstrating strong scalability.

### 4.5 Generalization and Robustness
A controller trained with annotations from one VLM (e.g., GPT-4o) maintained stable scores (9.2–10.2) when driven by a different VLM planner (e.g., Qwen-VL). Furthermore, instruction-following accuracy on unseen phrasing reached 86%–97% (average 92.8%), demonstrating remarkable robustness.

captions.F4: Controller training losses on Minecraft Diamond (200M model). Reconstruction, dynamics, policy, and value losses converge stably alongside the hindsight behavior cloning (bc) and stop prediction (stop) losses.

sections.heading: How It Differs from Existing VLAs and Hierarchical RL
sections.summary: While separating slow thinking from fast control is an established paradigm in robotics, this work distinguishes itself by using natural language as the common interface and relying on a world-model controller that requires zero expert demonstrations.
sections.details:
Decoupling deliberate thinking (System 2) from fast reactive control (System 1) has been studied extensively in autonomous driving, manipulation, and navigation (e.g., HiRT). However, this work sets itself apart in three key ways:

First, it uses open-ended natural language as the interface between planner and controller rather than latent embeddings or coordinate targets. This enables pretrained VLMs to be swapped in plug-and-play without fine-tuning, while naturally unlocking human-in-the-loop collaboration and multi-agent coordination via chat.

Second, using a world-model controller rather than a domain-specific waypoint follower allows the method to generalize across widely diverse observation and action spaces, from retro games to 3D navigation.

Third, unlike Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models such as SayCan, RT-2, or OpenVLA that depend on massive human demonstrations or domain-specific fine-tuning, Instruct-to-Act builds a language-guided controller entirely from scratch by summarizing its own RL rollouts with a VLM.

sections.heading: Toward a New Standard Architecture for Language-Driven Autonomous Agents
sections.summary: Instruct-to-Act establishes a unified framework combining high-frequency world-model control and high-level VLM reasoning via natural language. Future directions include direct human-in-the-loop guidance and training a single multi-task controller across diverse environments.
sections.details:
Instruct-to-Act brings together the best of both worlds: the flexible reasoning of VLMs and the low-latency, precise continuous execution of world-model RL. Experiments across seven environments prove that agents can solve complex tasks at high control frequencies and achieve multi-agent coordination without specialized MARL training.

Promising next steps include exploring interactive agents guided by real-time human prompts, asymmetric agent roles (e.g., commander and worker), and training a single unified multi-task controller rather than training per-environment models. By offering a practical, scalable blueprint for translating high-level language guidance into long-horizon low-level actions, this work provides valuable insights for the embodied AI community.

sections.heading: Appendix: Prompt Design and Asynchronous Buffer Synchronization
sections.summary: The appendix provides details on the shared asynchronous buffer mechanisms that minimize inference latency, as well as the concrete prompt templates used for single-agent and multi-agent VLM reasoning.
sections.details:
### Concurrency Control in Asynchronous Execution
To prevent observation-instruction mismatches between planner and controller, shared states (Inbox, Stop, Plan) are maintained in step-indexed buffers. When the controller writes an event exceeding the stop threshold $p_{\text{stop}}$, the planner—which has been reasoning in the background—only executes a quick "emit" step to decode a short instruction from its latest draft plan and writes it atomically to the Inbox. This asymmetry between heavy reasoning (advance) and lightweight issuance (emit) ensures smooth instruction switches without dropping control frequency.

### Prompt Design
The single-agent prompt (Figure 6) maintains reasoning memory $M_r$ and partial plans $P_n$ in JSON format, enforcing concise, verifiable command outputs (6–18 tokens) to keep the controller responsive. The multi-agent prompt (Figure 7) extends this with messaging capabilities (under 25 tokens, structured around claiming subgoals or reporting obstacles), enabling natural collaborative behaviors through chat.

captions.F7: Supplementary prompt for multi-agent coordination. It specifies communication protocols for decentralized and centralized modes, along with a JSON schema for sending concise subgoal claims and help requests under 25 tokens.

takeaways: Decoupling decision-making by having VLMs emit sparse text instructions for a world-model controller to execute yields major gains in both task performance and inference speed compared to direct VLM control.
Self-supervised hindsight relabeling—summarizing RL rollouts with a VLM—trains open-ended language-following controllers without requiring any human demonstrations.
Asynchronous inference, which separates heavy planner reasoning from fast instruction issuance, maintains high control frequencies regardless of VLM generation latency.
Multi-agent coordination can be achieved purely through natural language chat between VLM planners, without centralized value functions or complex MARL algorithms.
limitations: Controllers currently require separate reinforcement learning per environment; a single general-purpose controller sharing one set of weights across all domains has not yet been achieved (showing ~10% performance drop on MineRL).
Controller training relies on Dreamer's RL rollouts and environment reward signals, meaning an alternative exploration mechanism is needed to acquire controllers in reward-free open worlds.
Part of the instruction-following evaluation relied on manual inspection by a single author and GPT-5.5 agreement checks, leaving room for more extensive, blinded multi-annotator studies.
